study.title: Leviticus 27 - Votes, redemption and total consecration to the LORD
study.overview: Leviticus 27 works as a final appendix to the book and deals with voluntary vows made to the Lord. The chapter shows that spontaneous devotion was not left to the religious impulse: there was evaluation, ransom allowed in certain cases, an increase of one fifth and distinction between what could be reacquired and what was irrevocably consecrated. The text concludes by remembering that these commandments were given through Moses on Mount Sinai, reaffirming his divine authority and his place in the whole covenant.

outline.title: Evaluation of people voted for the LORD
outline.explanation: The chapter begins by dealing with people who are dedicated by vote. The evaluation varied according to age and sex, and the priest adjusted the value for those who were poor, showing that consecration was serious, but also fair and proportional to the real capacity of those who voted.

outline.title: Animals offered and possibility of rescue
outline.explanation: Animals suitable for sacrifice, once dedicated, became saints and could not be exchanged. Unclean animals could be evaluated and, if the owner wanted to rescue them, he should add a fifth, preserving the moral weight of the vote and discouraging levian decisions.

outline.title: Houses and fields
outline.explanation: The text extends the discussion for real estate. Houses and fields could be consecrated, assessed by the priest and, in some cases, rescued with an addition of a fifth. The Jubilee regulated the value of the fields as the remaining time, and certain lands returned to the original possessor, revealing that human possession was limited before the sovereignty of the LORD over the earth.

outline.title: Measures, firstborn, consecrated things and tithes
outline.explanation: The final section standardizes the valuations by the siclo of the sanctuary, protects the firstborn already belonging to the Lord, regulates unclean animals, distinguishes what is irrevocably consecrated and closes with the tithe of the land and the flock. The closure sums up the chapter as commandments God given to Moses for Israel in Sinai.

study.context: The chapter is presented as a conclusion of the book and, according to the notes, it acts as an increase that deals with votes and voluntary offers, alongside the instructions given on times and properties. The mention of Mount Sinai in the final verse indicates that the legislation belongs to the framework of the covenant and is not just devotional advice. The notes also note that in the ancient world there were violent pagan religious practices, but here consecration to the Lord is regulated without human sacrifice, preserving the value of life and the holiness of vow.
study.theology: Leviticus 27 teaches that devotion to God is neither improvised nor manipulable. The vow is a matter of responsibility before the LORD, and the law protects both the holiness of what has been consecrated and the integrity of the community. There is a strong principle of stewardship: people, animals, houses, fields, crops and flocks ultimately belong to God. The ransom with an addition of a fifth shows that the grace of readmission exists, but does not make the vote cheap. At the same time, the chapter distinguishes between only consecrated things and "consecrous" things, which cannot be reacquired, remembering that there are irreversible deliveries. The theology of the chapter also points to divine sovereignty over possession, work and worship: the people must honor the LORD with their possessions and with fidelity to the given word.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter closes the book and deals with various types of votes, with provision to rescue what was promised, showing what votes should be made carefully and fulfilled seriously.
The laws here deal with extraordinary and voluntary vows; God accepts what is sincerely offered, but also allows ransom at a certain price because people tend to repent of what they have promised.

The text organizes the evaluations of people, animals, houses and fields, regulating the value according to age, condition and circumstances, so that what was voted could be properly assessed by the priest.

questions: What do my promises to God reveal about the seriousness with which I deal with my word before him?
In which areas of my life do I recognize that everything already belongs to the Lord and not just a part of my time or of my money?
Am I offering to God what is left or what really expresses honor, gratitude, and obedience?
study.practice: Practice a more conscious and honest devotion: before making spiritual promises, think sobriety; fulfill what to say; if you need to correct a promise made without reflection, do it with humility and responsibility. In addition, read your resources, your home, your work and your abilities as gifts belonging to the Lord, using them faithfully, generously and ordained for worship, for Christian service and for the care of others.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text presented already brings the numbering and formulation in Portuguese, but some notions of the chapter depend on technical terms and evaluation regulations that do not appear in detail outside the chapter itself. The notes provided also suggest some historical and pastoral interpretations, but these should be read as interpretative explanations, not as absolute statements of the text. It is not possible to go beyond what the notes allow about dates, geography or exact practice of the cult in each case.
